To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

E6 functions in p53 degradation are necessary for stable replication of the HPV31 episome, but not sufficient, and that E6 and/or E7 functions that are independent of p53 degradation may also contribute to episomal replication.

1) the functions of the E6 and E6 proteins are required for episomal maintenance and 2) the balance of E6 and 7 activities in infected cells is important for episomal maintenance in primary human keratinocytes.

(i) the HPV E7 protein, in addition to the E6 protein, is required for the stable maintenance of HPV genomes in primary human keratinocytes; and (ii) E6 and E2 proteins, in addition to E1, are required for the transient replication of HPV genomes in keratinocytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that control the life cycle of human papillomaviruses, a large group of small DNA tumour viruses that infect the squamous epithelium.
the mechanisms of human papillomaviruses, a group of small DNA viruses associated with benign skin and mucosal warts and with cancers of the cervix and other mucosal surfaces.
the replication of human papillomaviruses (HPVs), small DNA viruses that are the causative agents of cervical cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
E6 is necessary for episomal replication of high-risk HPV in primary human keratinocytes.
the E6 and E1 proteins are essential for the maintenance of HPV genomes in primary human keratinocytes.
HPV16 E6 and E6* proteins are necessary for episome maintenance of the HPV16 genomes in keratinocytes, and that the p53 degradation activity of HPV16 E is not necessary for episomal replication.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the balance of E6 and the E7 function is critical for the episomal maintenance of human papillomaviruses.
we show that the balance between p53 and pRB degradation is critical for episome maintenance.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the balance of E6 and the E7 functions are important for HPV genome maintenance.
